item.title: Trump Orders Warnings Placed at ‘Inaccurate’ Smithsonian History Museum
item.description:
President Trump on Friday ordered warning signs and exhibits installed outside the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History to alert the public that the museum does not, in his view, accurately reflect American history.

The unusual directive, made through an executive order, was a considerable escalation of the president’s dispute with the Smithsonian and its history museum, which was the subject of a recent 162-page report. The report accused the museum’s director, Anthea M. Hartig, of “radical activist ideology” and the museum of undermining “faith in American institutions.”

The order went so far as to suggest that the signage inform potential museum visitors of locations where American history is better presented. The administration did not explain where the public would be redirected.

The Smithsonian declined to comment.

Mr. Trump’s order came just days after Ms. Hartig was grilled by Republican legislators in two congressional hearings, where she was accused of teaching “national self-loathing.”

Ms. Hartig, who was a particular target of the White House report, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In the hearings she contested the thrust of the report and insisted her museum was simply representing history in all its complexity.

“When historians talk about reframing a traditional narrative, we don’t mean erasing it,” she said in her testimony. “We mean adding the evidence, the voices, the objects that earlier tellings left out so that more Americans can see themselves reflected in the national story.”

Friday’s executive order also ordered several government officials to “restore trust in the Smithsonian Institution” and to seek its compliance with the White House findings, which asserted that the museum had become a tool of political activism and had not done enough to celebrate the achievements of the nation’s founders on the country’s 250th anniversary year.

The government officials include the interior secretary, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, the administrator of general services, and the assistant to the president for domestic policy, the order says. The Domestic Policy Council published the White House’s report on the Smithsonian.

The inclusion of the budget office is consistent with the White House remarks in other settings that pointed to the fact that the Smithsonian is largely federally funded.

Representative Melanie Stansbury, Democrat of New Mexico, was among those who objected to Mr. Trump’s effort.

“Once again, the Trump administration is attempting to use executive authority to exercise its political will over our nation’s independent cultural institutions,” she said in a statement. “This executive order is a clear political overreach, driven by an ideological agenda to rewrite American history. Our Smithsonian institutions do not belong to the president, but the American people, and so does our national story.”

Some historians have also criticized the federal government’s attempts to overhaul the Smithsonian as ideologically motivated.

“I cannot recall a single instance where exhibits have been directly wrestled with by the upper echelons of the federal government,” said Samuel J. Redman, a history professor at the University of Massachusetts Amherst who has written extensively on the Smithsonian’s history.

The order by the president said the signage “shall notify visitors that the museum exhibits should be renovated consistent with the findings in the report and direct visitors to locations and resources for accurate information regarding America’s history.”

“Because the museum has failed to appropriately honor the 56 signers of the Declaration of Independence during this 250th anniversary year of the founding of our country,” the order continues, government agencies “shall install temporary exhibits or signage on N.P.S.-maintained sidewalks, walkways, and land used by the public that corrects inaccurate information presented in the museum.”

In Friday’s order, Mr. Trump cited his March 2025 executive order, “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History,” which accused the Smithsonian of undermining “the remarkable achievements of the United States by casting its founding principles and historical milestones in a negative light.”

This week’s hearings, which took place on Tuesday and Wednesday, increased the pressure on Ms. Hartig, who was questioned by lawmakers about exhibitions that they said indicated a liberal bias in emphasizing the country’s flaws and failing to adequately celebrate its achievements.

In particular, Ms. Hartig was repeatedly taken to task for two recent shows, one of which — “Entertainment Nation” — included explicit sexual imagery. Another, “Girlhood (It’s complicated),” discussed struggles with gender identity among young women.

Mike Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the Heritage Foundation who has written critically about the Smithsonian and testified at both hearings, commended Friday’s executive order for enlisting the oversight of administration officials like Russell T. Vought, the White House budget director, and Vince Haley, the director of the White House’s Domestic Policy Council.

“Since I think the only way to correct the Smithsonian is to remove from office its entire leadership,” Mr. Gonzalez said, “I trust these two intellectual heavy hitters will work to do that.”

But Dr. Redman, the historian, said that many observers have been dismayed by the aggressiveness of the White House efforts to take control of the Smithsonian and its 21 museums.

“Historians are appalled,” Dr. Redman said. “The Smithsonian has been known for trying to present a consensus version of history.”

item.title: Whatever Happened to the B+ Student?
item.description:
To the Editor:

Re “Confessions of a Grade Inflater,” by Frank Bruni (Opinion, July 14):

After 41 years as a full-time professor at the University of Southern California, I empathize with Mr. Bruni’s predicament of being under pressure to inflate his students’ grades. Yet the most agonizing moments of my teaching career — spanning freshman seminars to doctoral and executive education — have come when I was facing the spreadsheet of final composite scores, rank-ordering my undergraduate students to assign letter grades.

I have painfully watched some of my best student thinkers — not necessarily my best test takers — fall victim to the tyranny of numbers. Some deserved a solid A, but lifeless figures, invoked in the name of resisting grade inflation, forced my hand. I still repent of it; one of my best former students, Jose, who stayed in touch with me, has heard my confession multiple times and has graciously forgiven me.

I believe that my best teaching happens in my freshman seminar on technology and the environment, graded pass/no pass. Freed from fear for their grade-point average, students engage fiercely, collaborate and challenge me and one another. Socrates is said to have observed that he could not teach people anything, but only make them think. No spreadsheet or final grade can ever measure that.

Let’s figure out a way for undergraduates to enjoy their learning and challenge themselves and their professors without dreading a final grade — at best a weak indicator of their potential.

Najmedin MeshkatiLos AngelesThe writer is a professor of engineering and international relations at the University of Southern California.

To the Editor:

We must be cautious when decrying grade inflation. The common assumption is that rising grades reflect diminishing faculty standards. However, because elite schools now matriculate a much smaller, hyper-selective fraction of applicants, student capability has vastly risen. Unless exams are deliberately engineered to be harder, grades reflecting true accomplishment should naturally increase.

Having recently retired after teaching master’s and undergraduate students at Yale for over 30 years, I can make an apples-to-apples comparison. My exam questions evolved over the decades, but they did not become easier. Would it make sense to artificially award lower grades for the same level of achievement today just to preserve a decades-old distribution curve? If we refuse to do so, it is not because grades are inflated; it is because quality has improved.

Gaboury BenoitNew Haven, Conn.The writer is an emeritus professor of environmental chemistry at the Yale School of the Environment.

To the Editor:

Frank Bruni identifies a symptom, but mistakes it for the disease.

Grade deflation might restore some rigor to university education, but it treats grading as a calibration problem when the deeper issue is atmospheric: We’ve built an education system in which students and their families are customers, learning is transactional and “success” has been reduced to a score.

Here’s my invitation to Mr. Bruni and anyone else working with young people: Stop fixating on grades, and start inviting students to define and live their own vision of excellence.

Benjamin Zander, the conductor and educator, famously gives every student an A on the first day of class. Not because they’ve earned it, but because now their job is to become the person who does. We use a version of this at the Flight School, the community I lead for young people navigating the transition to adulthood outside traditional institutions. It’s not permissiveness. It’s a different kind of rigor — one that challenges students to know what they know, without relying on others to validate it.

Capping A’s might hit the target, but it will still miss the point. Grades can measure only what’s measurable. The learning that matters most — awareness, aliveness, courage — rarely is.

We’ll forget most of what we learn in a classroom. But the knowing remains. The real assignment is teaching to that.

Abby FalikBerkeley, Calif.The writer is a founder of the Flight School and a visiting fellow at Stanford.

To the Editor:

Frank Bruni is right that grade inflation has drained the A of meaning, but I’d locate the solution elsewhere. Capping A’s at a fixed share of each class treats the grade as a scarce commodity and revives norm-referenced grading — ranking students against one another rather than against clear, shared standards. That comparison-based approach is its own distortion: A student’s mark ends up depending on who else is in the room.

The harder, more honest fix is defining what A-level work actually looks like across a department and grading against it. Such transparent criteria would also ease the uncomfortable grading conversations Mr. Bruni describes, turning a disputed mark from a personal negotiation into a shared look at the evidence.

Nor is this only a college problem. In my work preparing future teachers, I regularly hear how mentor teachers fold homework, participation, timeliness and behavior into grades — things that don’t measure what a student knows and can do. The answer is clearer standards, not tighter quotas.

Howard YankCamas, Wash.The writer is an emeritus faculty member of the College of Education at Portland State University.

To the Editor:

Awkward conversations between students and professors aren’t the only consequence of giving a student less than an A. The complaints escalate, involving the department chair and often the dean of students. Hours are wasted, as students, and sometimes their parents, haggle and whine until they receive that holy grail, an unblemished A. My husband’s chairman finally instructed him to do what he had to do to stop the time-wasting.

I taught as an adjunct instructor for 22 years, and so my position was much more precarious than that of my tenured husband. If my students thought that their grades were not sufficiently high, then their evaluations of me tanked, and I could be fired, with no recourse. Even when students plagiarized, I was supposed to give them a chance to rewrite their papers, with no penalty.

Needless to say, we are both delighted that we are no longer teaching. But I have one question for Frank Bruni: Do any of today’s students ever receive a C?

Barbara BarranBrooklyn

To the Editor:

The appropriate answer to grade inflation is not grading on a curve, deciding before a course begins what percentage of students can receive an A. That policy confuses rank in class with mastery of subject.

Rather, the problem can be solved simply by adjusting transcripts to include not only a student’s grade but also the average grade for all students in that section of the course. This way grade inflation is exposed and rendered pointless.

Steven M. CahnOld Greenwich, Conn.The writer is a professor emeritus of philosophy and former acting president at the City University of New York Graduate Center, and the author of “Towards Teaching Philosophy.”
